agree.reason: The page refuses to promise an A1C drop and offers a low-risk $59 trial and a call with the dietitian, so this wary reader is likely to try a week, though nothing speaks directly to their history of quitting within two months.

honest.reason: The A1C claim is cut back to what the 14 results support and the missing medication data is admitted, but 'nothing to cancel beyond that week' suggests the trial doesn't renew automatically, and the brief doesn't say that.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out the $12.90 per-meal price, but it leaves out the true 0.6-point average drop, never turns 10 of 14 or 37 of 88 (about 42% past six months) into shares, and puts the retention numbers in a section headed 'What I've seen, and what I can't promise' rather than tying them to staying power.

right_comparison.reason: The only alternative described is a vague 'cooking it every day'; the page never sets the 37 customers who stayed six months against this reader's pattern of quitting apps and services within a couple of months.

qualification.reason: The A1C hedge names real uncertainties the reader can understand (a small group, medication changes not tracked), but it gives no checkable threshold or timeframe, such as asking for an A1C test after three months.

objections.reason: It deals with skepticism about health promises, boredom, contracts and cost, but it never directly asks why this would last when other services didn't, though the facts on retention, swaps and the call could answer that.

fit.reason: It is a clear sales page of roughly 420 words with a single trial-week call to action, close to what the brief asked for.
